80	A **ROW** is an object with every field of that table, using the field names exactly as in the schema. Each field maps to a **cell**:
81	
82	```json
83	{"value": <value>, "span": "<exact quote from the paper>"}
84	```
85	
86	### Values
87	- **Type.** Use the schema's type for each field. Enum fields take only the listed strings.
88	- **Missing values.** Follow each field's schema description.
89	  - Where the description says "null", use `{"value": null, "span": null}`.
90	  - Otherwise, text and enum fields take `{"value": "not reported", "span": null}`, and numeric, date and boolean fields take `{"value": null, "span": null}`.
91	- **`pmid` fields.** The value comes from the header line; the span is that header line, e.g. `"PMID: 12345678"`.
92	- **`*_iso8601` fields.** These are your conversion of the matching original-text field. Give them only when the original text states a number, and use the same span as the original-text field.
93	- **`hpo_label_candidate` and `hpo_id_candidate`.** These are your suggestions. Give an ID only if you are sure of it; otherwise null. Their span is `null`.
94	- **`checklist_feature`.** The span is `null`, because the names come from the schema.
95	- **Age at diagnosis.** Record it in `age_at_diagnosis_*`. Don't put it in onset or last evaluation.
96	
97	### Spans
98	- **Every non-missing value needs a span**, except the fields listed just above.
99	- **Copy exactly.** A span is copied character for character from the paper Markdown, including unusual spaces and symbols. Never paraphrase, correct or join text that isn't contiguous.
100	- **Keep it short.** Use the smallest sentence fragment, table cell or table-row segment that supports the value. That is normally under 300 characters.
101	- **Tables with patients as rows.** Quote a contiguous piece of the row from the patient label through the cell.
102	- **Tables with patients as columns.** Quote the row from its row label through that patient's cell, e.g. `| Sex | F | M` for the second patient column. Name the column header once in `method_note`.
103	- **Multiple places.** If support sits in several places, `span` may be a list of exact quotes:
104	  - up to **five** for `treatment_summary`, `functional_evidence_statement`, `parental_testing_statement` and `clinical_diagnosis_basis`;
105	  - up to **three** for any other field.
106	
107	### Rows
108	- **`publications`:** exactly one row for this paper.
109	- **`individuals`:** one row per in-scope person (see Scope), labelled by the Labels rules.
110	- **`variants`:** one row per (person, variant).
111	  - `variant_original_string` is the **shortest** contiguous text giving the variant, not a whole sentence. Put the transcript, cDNA and protein parts in their own fields.
112	  - **(v3)** If the paper ties a *TNFAIP3* variant to the person but prints no variant description (only in a figure or an unavailable supplement), keep the row with `variant_original_string` = `"not reported"`. Never fill it from memory.
113	- **`phenotypic_features`:** one row per feature the paper explicitly reports present (`observed`) or explicitly reports absent (`excluded`) for that person. No rows for features the paper doesn't mention.
114	- **`phenotype_checklist`:** for **every** individual, one row for **each** of the 20 checklist features in the schema's description of that table, using the names exactly as listed there. Status is `observed`, `excluded` or `not reported` under rule 4.
115	
116	### Absence and evidence basis (D-21, D-22)
117	- **`evidence_basis` is required** on every `phenotypic_features` row, and on every checklist row whose status is not `not reported`.
118	- **Group statements.** You may mark a feature `excluded` for a person from a statement about a group **only when the statement names the group explicitly**, e.g. "only Pt3 of the four patients had recurrent fevers". Such rows take `evidence_basis = "inferred from group statement"`.
119	  - Counts without names ("arthritis in 2/4") do not exclude anyone.
120	- **(v3) Table symbols.** A `-`, `–`, `0`, `N` or similar cell counts as `excluded` only when the paper's legend or text defines that symbol as absent or negative.
121	  - Quote that definition as a second span next to the cell.
122	  - Otherwise the cell is `not reported` (rule 6). Empty cells, `NA` and `ND` are always `not reported`.
123	- **(v3) Study criteria are not evidence.** Never use a study's inclusion or exclusion criteria (e.g. "patients with malignancy were excluded") to mark a feature for a person.
124	- **Narrow and broad features.** A narrower absence never excludes a broader checklist item. "No arthritis" does not exclude "arthritis or arthralgia"; leave that item `not reported` unless arthralgia is also addressed. The same applies to other composite items, e.g. "skin lesions (rash, folliculitis, erythema nodosum)".
125	- **(v5, D-27) Normal findings.** When the paper reports a finding as normal or negative for a person ("CRP was normal", "normal C3 and C4 levels", "ANA negative"), record the abnormality it rules out as the feature and mark it `excluded`: `feature_text_as_stated` = "elevated CRP", "low complement", "positive ANA". Keep the paper's own words in the span ("CRP was normal"). Name only an abnormality the finding measures; a normal examination or investigation as a whole ("gastrointestinal investigation was negative") excludes nothing more specific than what it names, so write it as the paper does and say so in `method_note`.
126	- **(v4) Zero counts.** A count of 0 in a table of counts (e.g. "0" or "0/2" in a column for a disease group) excludes no one, like any count without names. Text that names the group ("none of the patients had uveitis") still excludes.
127	- **(v6, D-31) Stacked cells.** A cell with several values separated by ` / ` lists values that were stacked on separate lines (often one per patient). **Do not assign them to people by position**, even when the number of values equals the number of people. Use a stacked value for a person only when the paper labels it for that person (for example "P1: 18 / P2: 24", or a sentence naming the person and the value). Otherwise record the field or checklist item as `not reported` for each person in that row, and say in `method_note` which table and columns were stacked. A value the same for every person in the row, printed once (not stacked), is not affected.
128	- **Contradictions inside the paper.** If the paper says both that a person has a feature and that they don't:
129	  - emit both `phenotypic_features` rows, each with its own span;
130	  - set that checklist item to `not reported`;
131	  - list the contradiction in `method_note`.

133	### Variant fields belong to this person's variant (v5, D-29)
134	Zygosity, inheritance, variant type, pathogenicity, ACMG criteria and functional evidence describe **one person's variant**. Fill them only from:
135	- this person's own table row or column, or a sentence that names this person or this exact variant; or
136	- a statement about a **named group that includes this person** and gives one value for all of them ("all six patients carried heterozygous variants").
137	
138	Leave the field `not reported` (with span null) when:
139	- the statement is about the cohort's or the paper's variants in general, without naming a group this person is clearly in ("the variants were classified as pathogenic");
140	- the statement lists several values for a group ("splice-site, frameshift and nonsense variants"): it does not say which one is this person's;
141	- the paper gives this person a different or open status elsewhere: a variant not identified or not determined, a mosaic or somatic finding, a VUS, a relative not tested. A group statement never overrides that;
142	- the value is about another person's variant, for example a relative carrying the proband's variant, unless the paper says it for the relative.
143	
144	Variant type: record only a class the paper states for this variant (or for a named group of variants that includes it). Do not derive it from the HGVS string.

150	- This is more specific than rule 8, so it wins.

2	PMCID: PMC13453388
3	DOI: 10.2147/IMCRJ.S587900
4	Title: Infantile Onset Haploinsufficiency of A20 Treated by Infliximab, a Case Report and Brief Review of Literature
5	Journal: International Medical Case Reports Journal (2026)
6	Authors: Salehzadeh Farhad; Babazadeh Khoei Faeze
7	
8	# Infantile Onset Haploinsufficiency of A20 Treated by Infliximab, a Case Report and Brief Review of Literature
9	
10	## Abstract
11	
12	AbstractBackgroundHaploinsufficiency of A20 (HA20) is a rare genetic autoinflammatory syndrome caused by heterozygous loss-of-function variants in TNFAIP3. It typically appears in early childhood with recurrent fevers, mucocutaneous ulcers, gastrointestinal symptoms, and occasional eye involvement. The overlapping features with Behçet disease and other autoinflammatory disorders often make diagnosis challenging.Case PresentationWe describe a 5-year-old girl who developed periodic fevers from age 2, along with oral ulcers, eye redness and swelling, abdominal pain, diarrhea, perianal tenderness, and dysuria. Initial treatments with colchicine and intermittent prednisolone provided little benefit. Whole exome sequencing revealed a likely pathogenic variant in TNFAIP3 (TNFAIP3 Chr6 138197257 138197257 C: NM_001270507.2: (5/9): c.759delC: p. Asp253fs), consistent with a diagnosis of Behçet-like autoinflammatory syndrome (HA20), with additional variants in PIK3R1, HBB, and SERPINA1 possibly modifying the phenotype.Management and OutcomeAfter the genetic diagnosis, therapy was escalated to infliximab, which led to improvement, this highlights the effectiveness of targeted biologic therapy in refractory pediatric HA20 insufficiency who unresponsive to conventional therapies.Keywords: haploinsufficiency of A20, TNFAIP3, infliximab
13	
14	## Introduction
15	
16	Haploinsufficiency of A20 (HA20) is a recently recognized monogenic autoinflammatory and immune-dysregulation syndrome caused by heterozygous loss-of-function variants in the TNFAIP3 gene, which encodes the ubiquitin-editing protein A20.^1 A20 is a critical negative regulator of NF-κB signaling and other proinflammatory pathways, acting via both deubiquitinase and E3 ligase activities to limit excessive innate and adaptive immune activation.^2 HA20 was first described in 2016 in patients from multiple unrelated families who presented with early-onset systemic inflammation resembling Behçet disease; subsequent reports and case series have expanded the recognized clinical and genetic spectrum.^3 Symptoms of HA20 most often begin in early childhood, typically before the age of five, although some patients may present as early as infancy or later in adolescence, highlighting the broad variability in disease onset and expression.^3^,^4
17	
18	Clinically, HA20 shows marked phenotypic heterogeneity but is commonly characterized by recurrent oral and genital aphthae, episodic fever, cutaneous lesions, gastrointestinal inflammation, arthralgia/arthritis, and variable involvement of the eyes.^5
19	
20	Skin involvement is diverse and occurs in about 40% to 50% of HA20 patients. Common findings include folliculitis-like and acneiform lesions, psoriasiform rashes, erythema nodosum, vasculitis lesions and dermal abscesses. Ocular manifestations include uveitis, retinal vasculitis scleritis and episcleritis although are less common than skin involvement, affecting roughly 7% to 10% of HA20 patients, these manifestations can be severe and require aggressive immunosuppression.^5
21	
22	Patients may also show features of autoimmunity (for example lupus-like or rheumatoid manifestations) and, less commonly, immunodeficiency. Because of overlapping signs, HA20 may be misdiagnosed as Behçet disease or other systemic autoimmune/autoinflammatory disorders.^6 At the molecular level, haploinsufficiency (reduced dose) of A20 leads to impaired termination of NF-κB activation and dysregulated ubiquitin signaling, resulting in increased production of proinflammatory cytokines (eg, TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6) and enhanced responses to TLR and TNF stimuli.^4 Therapeutically, management is individualized and often includes corticosteroids and conventional immunosuppressants; biologic agents targeting cytokines (for example anti-TNF or IL-1 pathway inhibitors) have been used with benefit in refractory cases.^3 Ongoing accumulation of genotype–phenotype and treatment-response data are helping to refine clinical care and to identify when targeted biologic therapy is indicated.
23	
24	We describe a 5-year-old girl who developed periodic fevers from age 2, along with oral ulcers, eye redness and swelling, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and perianal tenderness. WES revealed a pathogenic variant in TNFAIP3 with additional variants in PIK3R1, HBB, and SERPINA1 possibly modifying the phenotype.
25	
26	## Case Presentation
27	
28	A five-year-old Caucasian consanguine girl presented to our clinic with a history of recurrent periodic fever from the age of second year. Each febrile episode occurred every 20 days and lasted approximately three days. During these episodes, she experienced redness and pain in the eyes, swelling of the upper and lower eyelids, abdominal pain, oral aphthous ulcers, diarrhea, perianal tenderness and swelling, and dysuria. Her parents reported that these symptoms had persisted despite supportive care. Gastrointestinal evaluation did not reveal findings suggestive of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD).
29	
30	Her past medical history was significant for a full-term birth complicated by neonatal distress syndrome. During early infancy, the patient had a brief febrile convulsive seizure, following neurological workup. She was treated with phenobarbital for four months because of early infancy and convulsive type of seizure, and no further seizures occurred afterward. On examination during febrile episodes, periorbital swelling aphthous ulcers abdominal tenderness, and the perianal area was swollen and tender, resembling hemorrhoidal inflammation were shown. The patient’s initial and comprehensive investigations work has been shown in Table 1.
31	
32	### Table 1: Laboratory Investigations
33	
34	| Laboratory Parameter | Result | Laboratory Parameter | Result |
35	|---|---|---|---|
36	| White Blood Cells (WBC) | 8.62 ×10^9/L | AST | 23 U/L |
37	| Neutrophil | 4.81 ×10^9/L | ALT | 12 U/L |
38	| Lymphocyte | 3.06 ×10^9/L | ALP | 408 U/L |
39	| Hemoglobin | 10.6 g/dL | ESR (1 hour) | 14 mm/hr |
40	| Platelets | 391 ×10^9/L | CRP | Weakly Positive |
41	| Ferritin | 28 ng/mL | PPD | Negative |
42	| BUN | 20 mg/dL | Urinalysis (U/A) | Normal |
43	| Celiac serology | Negative | Urine Culture (U/C) | No growth |
44	| MEFV gene mutations | Negative | Creatinine (Cr) | 0.6 mg/dL |
45	| IgA | 162 mg/dL | IgM | 125 mg/dL |
46	| IgG | 1677 mg/dL | ANA | Negative |
47	| C3 & C4 | Normal | NBT | Normal |
48	
49	Given the recurrent nature of the fevers, the initial differential diagnoses included PFAPA syndrome and familial Mediterranean fever (FMF). Her ophthalmologic and Gastrointestinal investigation (including imaging and stool calprotectin) were negative. She was started on colchicine and intermittent courses of prednisolone, but these treatments did not lead to meaningful improvement in her fevers or mucocutaneous symptoms. The patient was also tested for familial Mediterranean fever (FMF) 12 common MEFV gene variant alleles, which returned negative, helping to rule out this common autoinflammatory differential diagnosis. Whole exome sequencing (WES) was performed (Whole Exome Sequencing was performed by NextSeq500, Twist Bioscience, San Francisco, CA, 100X, and Variant calling based on best practice of GATK. Genome ref version V. B37GRCh37.) due to the patient’s atypical presentation and poor response to conventional therapy. The analysis identified a likely pathogenic variant in TNFAIP3 (TNFAIP3 Chr6 138197257 138197257 C: NM_001270507.2: (5/9): c.759delC: p. Asp253fs), consistent with a diagnosis of Behçet-like autoinflammatory syndrome (HA20). Additional variants were detected in PIK3R1, HBB, and SERPINA1, which were considered to play a potential modifier role but were not thought to be the primary cause of her symptoms. A variant of uncertain significance (VUS) was also reported in VPS37A. We planned to confirm these variants in the patient and parents by Sanger sequencing, but some unpredictable limitations delayed that.
50	
51	The identification of the TNFAIP3 variant directly guided clinical management. Based on this molecular diagnosis, the patient’s therapy was escalated to include infliximab, at a dose of 5 mg/kg administered at weeks 0, 2, and 6, followed by maintenance infusions every eight weeks. Colchicine was discontinued and corticosteroids were tapered, which led to significant clinical improvement, highlighting the value of genetic testing in guiding targeted treatment in complex autoinflammatory syndromes.
52	
53	## Discussion
54	
55	Haploinsufficiency of A20 (HA20) is increasingly recognized as a monogenic autoinflammatory/immune-dysregulation syndrome with onset often in childhood.^5 Based on authors knowledge this is the first report from northeast of Iran. In multiple reported cohorts, early presentations include recurrent fevers, mucocutaneous ulcerations, gastrointestinal symptoms, skin lesions, and joint manifestations. In a recent systematic review of 177 HA20 patients, mucosal ulcers were among the most frequent findings (in ~129 of 177), followed by fever, gastrointestinal and skin involvement. Thus, the classic childhood phenotype often overlaps strongly with Behçet-like presentations.^7
56	
57	In many reports, patients had disease onset in early childhood or even infancy, with recurrent mucosal ulcers, fever, gastrointestinal ulcerations, and systemic inflammation. Some articles compared HA20 with classical Behçet disease and emphasized that high fever flares and digestive involvement beginning in early life appear as hallmarks of HA20 compared to adult-onset Behçet disease. Behçet disease is non-periodic multisystem inflammatory vasculitis. It is not caused by a single gene. Risk is influenced by HLA-B51, environmental triggers, and immune dysregulation. Symptoms usually begin in adults (20–40 years).^8 Moreover, others reported that among HA20 patients, disruption of the ZnF domain (zinc-finger) correlates with earlier onset (median ~2.5 years) compared to OTU domain mutations, suggesting genotype–phenotype associations.^9
58	
59	Thus, in reported cases, the childhood features often include recurrent periodic or episodic fevers, Painful oral (and sometimes genital) ulcers, Gastrointestinal inflammation, diarrhea, abdominal pain, Skin lesions (folliculitis, erythema, purpura), arthralgia/arthritis, occasionally ocular involvement (uveitis, conjunctivitis), variable autoimmunity or autoantibodies in some patients (ANA, anti-dsDNA), elevated inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR) during flares. In the systematic review of 177 cases, 93 had fever, 81 had GI inflammation, and 129 had mucosal ulcers (oral and/or genital). One difference in our case is the presence of perianal swelling resembling hemorrhoidal inflammation and dysuria, which are less commonly emphasized in the published HA20 literatures. Perianal involvement, as observed in our patient, is less commonly emphasized in published HA20 literature but may represent an extension of gastrointestinal mucosal inflammation or perianal soft-tissue involvement;^10 while genitourinary symptoms (dysuria) are less frequently reported in HA20, they could reflect local inflammation or urinary tract irritation under systemic inflammatory settings. There are occasional reports of urinary tract involvement or genitourinary symptoms in autoinflammatory syndromes overlapping with HA20, but they are not as well characterized.
60	
61	Another distinguishing element is the infancy history: the patient had seizures in infancy with negative family history of seizure and phenobarbital therapy. To our knowledge, no consistent reports in HA20 literature emphasize such neurological complications as part of the disease spectrum, although neurological manifestations (CNS vasculitis, aseptic meningitis, neuropathy) have been reported in older patients.^5 Thus, this febrile seizure may represent a comorbid or coincidental event, or possibly an extreme manifestation of immune dysregulation in early life (though this is speculative).
62	
63	From the genetic perspective, this patient was found to carry probable pathogenic variants in TNFAIP3 (among others). This matches the molecular etiology of HA20, as ~95% of affected individuals carry heterozygous TNFAIP3 pathogenic variants. The presence of additional variants in PIK3R1, HBB, and SERPINA1 identified on whole-exome sequencing are generally secondary findings. They do not modify or explain the core HA20 phenotype, but they can influence clinical presentation, comorbidities, or management depending on whether they are pathogenic. The TNFAIP3 variant remains the disease-causing mutation.
64	
65	Given the phenotypic heterogeneity and absence of formal guidelines, therapy in HA20 is individualized. Common approaches include corticosteroids, conventional immunosuppressants, and biologic cytokine inhibitors (anti-TNF, anti-IL-1, etc).^3 In early reports, many patients were initially treated under misdiagnoses (eg, Behçet, lupus) with steroids or immunosuppressants until genetic diagnosis clarified management.^11
66	
67	In one of reports, writers noted that in their cohort, cytokine inhibitors enabled control of systemic inflammation in many patients; in 7 of 9 patients receiving biologics, inflammation was suppressed effectively.^3 In another report has been suggested that biotherapies such as anti-TNFα or anti-IL-1 may be preferred in refractory cases, as response to colchicine is unpredictable (only ~24% respond in HA20, in contrast to classical Behçet disease).^8
68	
69	In the systematic review of 177 cases, the most common treatments included corticosteroids, NSAIDs, colchicine, methotrexate, and TNF blockers (eg, infliximab, etanercept).^7 More recently, JAK inhibitors have been proposed in selected patients, especially where cytokine-driven inflammation is prominent.^7
70	
71	Initial management with colchicine was attempted, as it has been used in several HA20 and Behçet-like autoinflammatory cases to reduce mucocutaneous and febrile episodes by modulating neutrophil activity and inflammatory cytokine release.^3 However, our patient showed no meaningful improvement in the frequency or intensity of febrile attacks and mucosal lesions after several months of colchicine therapy.
72	
73	Given the partial or absent response, treatment was escalated to include the anti–TNF-α monoclonal antibody infliximab, which has demonstrated efficacy in multiple pediatric HA20 cases refractory to conventional immunosuppressants.^12 Following initiation of infliximab, the patient exhibited a marked clinical improvement, and only one self-limited febrile episode over an eight-month follow-up period. This favorable response aligns with previously reported outcomes in HA20 patients treated with biologic agents targeting TNF-α or IL-1 pathways, supporting the role of cytokine blockade as a rational, mechanism-based therapy in A20 deficiency–related autoinflammation.^1^,^5 Long-term monitoring will be necessary to assess sustained remission and potential adverse effects.
74	
75	There are currently no standardized treatment guidelines for HA20. Conventional therapies such as corticosteroids and colchicine often provide incomplete or transient benefits. Biologic agents targeting proinflammatory cytokines, particularly TNF-α and IL-1, have demonstrated efficacy in refractory cases.^3^,^7 The favorable response to infliximab in this patient further supports the role of targeted biologic therapy in pediatric HA20.
76	
77	Although limitations in genetic data may exist, recognition of the characteristic clinical phenotype and timely initiation of targeted biologic therapy support the diagnosis and management of patients.
78	
79	## Conclusion
80	
81	Haploinsufficiency of A20 (HA20) should be considered in children presenting with recurrent fevers, mucocutaneous ulcers, gastrointestinal involvement, and ocular symptoms, especially when conventional therapies fail. Early recognition and genetic confirmation are essential to guide targeted treatment and prevent complications. Biologic therapy, particularly anti–TNF agents like infliximab, can provide significant clinical benefit in refractory cases.
